title: 1 Samuel 30:21–31
context: When David returns to the two hundred men who stayed at the brook Besor, some worthless men among the fighters refuse to share the plunder with them, but David insists that what the LORD has given must be shared alike between those who fought and those who stayed with the baggage, and this becomes a statute in Israel. Back in Ziklag, David sends gifts from the plunder to the elders of Judah in many towns. Both traditions read this as shared ground on grace and generosity: the victory was the LORD’s gift, so no one can claim it as earned.

verses.text: David came to the two hundred men, who were so faint that they could not follow David, whom also they had made to stay at the brook Besor; and they went out to meet David, and to meet the people who were with him. When David came near to the people, he greeted them.
verses.arminianNotes:
David comes to the two hundred men left at the brook Besor, and they go out to meet him; he greets them. Arminian readers note David’s warmth toward those who could not continue.

He does not treat them as failures.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see David honoring the weak within the community.

The greeting prepares for his defense of their share in verses 23–24.

verses.text: Then all the wicked men and worthless fellows of those who went with David answered and said, “Because they didn’t go with us, we will not give them anything of the plunder that we have recovered, except to every man his wife and his children, that he may lead them away and depart.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Wicked and worthless men among those who went with David refuse to share the plunder, except returning wives and children. Arminian readers note that greed appears even after a gracious victory.

The narrator’s description of these men leaves no doubt about how the text views their attitude.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the selfishness of the human heart claiming as earned what was actually given.

The complaint denies that the victory was God’s gift, which David’s answer will correct.

verses.text: Then David said, “Do not do so, my brothers, with that which the LORD has given to us, who has preserved us, and delivered the troop that came against us into our hand.
verses.arminianNotes:
David says, “Do not do so, my brothers, with that which the LORD has given to us.” Arminian readers note that David grounds his ruling in God’s gift and protection.

He addresses even the grumblers as “my brothers.”
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see grace as the basis for generosity. What God has given cannot be hoarded as if earned.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the victory belonged to the LORD, who preserved them and delivered the enemy into their hand.

verses.text: Who will listen to you in this matter? For as his share is who goes down to the battle, so shall his share be who stays with the baggage. They shall share alike.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“For as his share is who goes down to the battle, so shall his share be who stays with the baggage. They shall share alike.” Arminian readers note the principle of equal sharing among all who serve.

Those who guard the supplies are honored with those who fight.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a principle that echoes earlier practice (Num 31:27; Josh 22:8) and fits the New Testament picture of different members serving one body (1 Cor 12:21–26), as an application.

Every role in God’s work is valued.

verses.text: It was so from that day forward that he made it a statute and an ordinance for Israel to this day.
verses.arminianNotes:
From that day David made it a statute and an ordinance for Israel “to this day.” Arminian readers note that the ruling became lasting law.

The phrase shows the narrator writing at a later time.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see David acting as a king establishing just order even before he takes the throne.

The statute reflects God’s justice and generosity embedded in Israel’s practice.

verses.text: When David came to Ziklag, he sent some of the plunder to the elders of Judah, even to his friends, saying, “Behold, a present for you from the plunder of the LORD’s enemies.”
verses.arminianNotes:
David sends some plunder to the elders of Judah as “a present for you from the plunder of the LORD’s enemies.” Arminian readers note David’s generosity toward those who had suffered from the raids (v. 14).

The gift also builds goodwill among Judah’s leaders.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see David acknowledging that the victory was over the LORD’s enemies.

Many note that these ties prepare for David’s anointing at Hebron by the men of Judah (2 Sam 2:1–4).

verses.text: He sent it to those who were in Bethel, to those who were in Ramoth of the South, to those who were in Jattir,
verses.arminianNotes:
Gifts go to Bethel, Ramoth of the South, and Jattir. Arminian readers note that the list names towns in the southern region where David had lived and moved.

This Bethel is probably not the northern Bethel, but its identification is uncertain.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see David honoring the places connected with his years as a fugitive.

The list shows David’s care for the wider community of Judah, not just his own band.

verses.text: to those who were in Aroer, to those who were in Siphmoth, to those who were in Eshtemoa,
verses.arminianNotes:
Gifts go to Aroer, Siphmoth, and Eshtemoa. Arminian readers note that these towns were in Judah’s southern territory, though some locations are uncertain.

The list continues David’s acts of generosity.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see David’s thoroughness in sharing the plunder.

Each named town represents people who had supported or sheltered him.

verses.text: to those who were in Racal, to those who were in the cities of the Jerahmeelites, to those who were in the cities of the Kenites,
verses.arminianNotes:
Gifts go to Racal and to the cities of the Jerahmeelites and the Kenites. Arminian readers note that David includes clans allied with Judah (cf. 1 Sam 27:10).

The Kenites had shown kindness to Israel in the past (1 Sam 15:6).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see David’s generosity reaching beyond Israel’s tribes to friendly peoples.

The inclusion of these clans reflects a wider circle of covenant goodwill.

verses.text: to those who were in Hormah, to those who were in Borashan, to those who were in Athach,
verses.arminianNotes:
Gifts go to Hormah, Borashan, and Athach. Arminian readers note Hormah’s earlier history (Num 21:3).

Some of these places cannot be located with confidence.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the continuing list of David’s gifts.

The names connect David’s present actions with Israel’s past in the land.

verses.text: to those who were in Hebron, and to all the places where David himself and his men used to stay.
verses.arminianNotes:
Gifts go to Hebron and to all the places where David and his men used to stay. Arminian readers note that Hebron will soon be the place where David is made king over Judah (2 Sam 2:1–4).

David remembers those who helped him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God preparing David’s way to the throne through gratitude and generosity.

The chapter ends with David’s thankful sharing, in contrast to the account of Saul’s death that follows.
